notes:
=== ENUMERATION TOOLSET OVERVIEW ===
Run the full toolset immediately after gaining a foothold. Don't wait — the order matters.

TOOL SELECTION DECISION TREE:
- winPEAS → broadest automated coverage, noisy, many false positives
- Seatbelt → C# host survey, checks ~50 security-relevant host settings
- SharpUp → focuses exclusively on privilege escalation misconfigs
- PowerUp → PowerShell-based, runs where C# tools are blocked
- Watson → kernel exploit detection by KB vs OS version
- WES-NG → offline alternative, run systeminfo output through it on attack host
- LaZagne → credential sweeper, dozens of application categories
- SessionGopher → targets remote access tool credential stores (PuTTY, WinSCP, RDP)

=== OPERATIONAL NOTES ===
Compile C# tools from source or use precompiled binaries — AV signatures differ significantly.
When AV is active, try obfuscated PowerShell variants before dropping binaries.
Run winPEAS and SharpUp results in parallel to cross-reference findings.
Always log full output to file: .\winPEAS.exe | Tee-Object winpeas-out.txt

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
Tool output feeds directly into subsequent exploitation:
winPEAS/SharpUp → identify weak ACL, unquoted paths, AlwaysInstallElevated
Seatbelt → identify LSASS protection mode, AppLocker config, AV state
Watson/WES-NG → identify missing KBs → select kernel exploit
LaZagne → credential harvest → lateral movement or domain escalation
SessionGopher → saved RDP/SSH creds → pivot to additional hosts

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
Non-standard tokens in whoami /priv (any beyond SeChangeNotify + SeIncreaseWorkingSet)
Group memberships beyond standard domain users
Installed third-party software (wmic product get name)
Services running as LocalSystem with modifiable binaries or registry keys
Missing patches (cross-ref KB list against Watson output) Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 16 (Windows Privilege Escalation).

recommended.note: Follow up on the missing-patch findings.
